newsitem.title: UK: London gold takes a breather after recent surge.
newsitem.headline: London gold takes a breather after recent surge.

text.p: Gold eased off the day's highs on Wednesday afternoon after maintaining a steady push into firmer territory since the start of the week.
Despite a more bullish mood and a gain of $4 an ounce over the past three days, gold appeared to encounter stiff resistance below the important $385 an ounce level, dealers said.

"I can't see gold getting up above $385," one said. The high bid quoted early on was $384.30 an ounce. But bullion fixed slightly weaker at $383.50 an ounce in the afternoon, compared to $383.95 in the morning.
Prices had started ticking higher after investment funds, most of them U.S-based, began covering their short positions early in the week, dealers said.
Despite market expectations of sharp declines, gold had stubbornly held above the key $380 support level over the past two weeks.

But dealers said gold may be unable to break out of a $380-$385 price range until after the end-of-month expiration of gold options, which give the right but not the obligation to buy or sell the metal at a given price.
"Actually, $385 isn't a technical level, it's just a round number. But it is significant because it's a key strike level for options," a dealer said.
In the event of gold breaking above $385 it would run into layers of stiff resistance between $386 and $388, which had provided buying support when prices were heading downhill.
Silver, like gold, came off the day's highs which just touched the psychologically important $5.00 an ounce level.
It was indicated one cent up from Tuesday's London close at $4.97/$4.99 an ounce.
"A lot depends on silver. If it started breaking down it would cap gold's rise. But a break above the key $5.09-$5.11 area would probably take it up to $5.20," a dealer said.
Platinum was $0.90 firmer at $386.75/$387.75 an ounce, while palladium was unchanged at $118.25/$119.25 after recovering from 3-1/2 year lows around $115 an ounce last week.
Dealers said the platinum group metals were absorbing strength from gold.
But recent political uncertainty in Russia, a key producer of platinum and palladium, was also helping to boost prices.
